Q. Non-verbal communication is an important part of social communication. Identify the different types of non-verbal communication in the following parts:
    (i) Identify and describe (in one or two sentences) ‘welcoming, threatening, and persuasive’ images from the following?(6)
Example: Image no.4 is identified as ‘caring’ and it represents one’s care and love. Image 1:

Threatening: the face of the girl is anxious which means the hands on her shoulder may cause her to feel at risk.
Image 2:

Persuasive: the man is speaking in a good mood. May be he is trying to persuade someone to do or believe something throughreasoning.
Image 3:

Welcoming: the man is behaving in a polite way to a guest or new arrival into his shop or home maybe.
Image 4:

Image no.4 is identified as ‘caring’ and it represents one’s care and love.
    (ii) Touching is a type of non-verbal communication which operates at many levels. Identify and describe (in one to two sentences) images which represent functional, professional, socio-political, friendship-warmth, and love-intimacy levels of touch.(10)
Example: Image no.4 is identified as ‘commitment level’ and it represents one’s promise to commit some act.
Image 1:

Love intimacy: the reason is because the touch in the picture shows the love of the mother and the son for each other.
Image 2:

Socio-Political touch… the picture above presents a crowd of a political meeting.

Image 3:

Love-intimacy: arrow in heart is used to present the falling in love or a new fling.

Image 4:

The image presents the ‘commitment level’ and it represents one’s promise to commit some act

Image 5:

Friendship-Warmth Touch. The reason is because the picture here presents two friends together.

Image 6:

Functional touch because a task is being performed in this image.
    (iii) Name and describe the type of touch in the context of following images.(4) Image 1:

“Physical conflict” are more limited in range than the other types of signals, as the picture here presents the two deer right next to each other in order to fight.
Image 2:

This picture has three different people using three different gestures. This type of touch is done during conversation to grab the attention of the viewer or the listener.

Q1: E-Dictionary OR or Developments in Electronic Dictionary Design

Compiled By Adeel

3
                           Eng502 Finals Compilation
An electronic dictionary is a dictionary whose data exists in digital form and can be accessed
through a number of different media.
Electronic dictionaries can be found in several forms, including:
     as dedicated handheld devices
     as apps on smartphones and tablet computers or computer software
     as a function built into an E-reader
As CD-ROMs and DVD-ROMs, they are typically packaged with a printed dictionary to be
installed on the user’s own computer. As free or paid-for online products most of the early
electronic dictionaries were print dictionaries made available in digital form. The content was
identical. But the electronic editions provided users with more powerful search functions. But
soon the opportunities offered by digital media began to be exploited.
Electronic dictionary databases, especially those included with software dictionaries are often

                                                      um
extensive and can contain up to 500,000 headwords and definitions, verb conjugation tables, and
a grammar reference section. Bilingual electronic dictionaries and monolingual dictionaries of
inflected languages often include an interactive verb conjugator, and are capable of word
stemming and lemmatization. Electronic dictionaries are also available in logographic and
rightto-left scripts, including Arabic, Persian, Chinese, Devanagari, Greek, Hebrew, Japanese,
Korean, and Thai. Several developers of the systems that drive electronic dictionary software

                                            nj
offer API and SDK – Software Development Kit tools for adding various language-based
functions to programs, and web services such as the AJAX API used by Google.

Q. E-Dictionary:

An electronic dictionary is a dictionary whose data exists in digital form and can be accessed
through a number of different media.

Electronic dictionaries can be found in several forms, including:

   as dedicated handheld devices

  as apps on smartphones and tablet computers or computer software

  as a function built into an E-reader

As CD-ROMs and DVD-ROMs, they are typically packaged with a printed dictionary to be
installed on the user’s own computer. As free or paid-for online products most of the early
electronic dictionaries were print dictionaries made available in digital form. The content was
identical. But the electronic editions provided users with more powerful search functions. But
soon the opportunities offered by digital media began to be exploited.

Electronic dictionary databases, especially those included with software dictionaries are often
extensive and can contain up to 500,000 headwords and definitions, verb conjugation tables, and

a grammar reference section. Bilingual electronic dictionaries and monolingual dictionaries of
inflected languages often include an interactive verb conjugator, and are capable of word
stemming and lemmatization. Electronic dictionaries are also available in logographic and right-
to-left scripts, including Arabic, Persian, Chinese, Devanagari, Greek, Hebrew, Japanese,
Korean, and Thai. Several developers of the systems that drive electronic dictionary software
offer API and SDK – Software Development Kit tools for adding various language-based
functions to programs, and web services such as the AJAX API used by Google.

Q. Stages of Child language learning:

The stages of language production by the children focusing primarily on the unfolding of lexical
and syntactic knowledge are mentioned as follows:

            Stage                         Typical Age                      Description Age
Babbling                          6-8 months                        Repetitive CV patterns
One- word stage(better one-       9-18 months                       Single open-class words or
morpheme or one- unit) or                                           word stems
holophrastic stage
Two-word stage                    18-24 months                      ‘mini-sentences’ with simple
                                                                    semantic relations
Telegraphic stage or early        24-30 months                      ‘Telegraphic’ sentence
multiword stage                                                     structures of lexical rather
                                                                    than functional or grammatical
                                                                    morphemes.
Later multiword stage             30+ months                        Grammatical or functional
                                                                    structure emerge.

Q. Two Phrase Structure Rule:

These are the rules that form phrases of different types e.g., noun phrase, verb phrase, and
adjective phrase etc. A tree diagram can have two different ways: simply as a static
representation of the structure of the sentence shown at the bottom of the tree diagram. Every
single sentence can have a tree diagram. The other one is the dynamic format which is a way of
generating not only that particular sentence, but a very large number of other sentences with
similar structures. This second approach is very appealing because it would enable us to generate
a very large number of sentences with what looks like a very small number of rules. These rules
are called phrase structure rules.

offer API and SDK – Software Development Kit tools for adding various language-based
functions to programs, and web services such as the AJAX API used by Google.

Q. Syntax (Topic 123)
The word ‘syntax’ comes originally from Greek and literally means ‘a putting together’ or
arrangement. There was an attempt to produce an accurate description of the sequence or ordering
‘arrangement’ of elements in the linear structure of the sentence. In the more recent attempts to
analyze syntactic structure, there has been a greater focus on the underlying rule system that we
used to produce or ‘generate’ sentences.
Q. Tree Diagram (Topic 133)
The most common way to create a visual representation of syntactic structures is through tree
diagrams. We can use the symbols introduced (Art=article, N = noun, NP = noun phrase) to label
parts of the tree as we try to capture the hierarchical organization of those parts in the underlying
structure of phrases and sentences. At the top of the tree diagram, we begin with a sentence (S),
and divide it into two constituents (NP and VP). In turn, the NP constituent is divided into two
other constituents (Art and N) and VP into V and NP. At the top of the tree diagram, we begin
with a sentence (S) and divide it into two constituents (NP and VP). In turn, the NP constituent is
divided into two other constituents (Art and N).
Q. Two Phrase Structure Rule: (Topic 134)
These are the rules that form phrases of different types e.g., noun phrase, verb phrase, and adjective
phrase etc. A tree diagram can have two different ways: simply as a static representation of the
structure of the sentence shown at the bottom of the tree diagram. Every single sentence can have
a tree diagram. The other one is the dynamic format which is a way of generating not only that
particular sentence, but a very large number of other sentences with similar structures. This second
approach is very appealing because it would enable us to generate a very large number of sentences
with what looks like a very small number of rules. These rules are called phrase structure rules.
These rules state that the structure of a phrase of a specific type will consist of one or more
constituents in a particular order. Phrase structure rules present the information of the tree diagram
in another format.
   ❖ S → NP VP
   ❖ NP → {Art (Adj) N, Pro, PN}
   ❖ VP → V NP (PP) (Adv)
   ❖ PP → Prep NP
Q. Types of Meaning (Topic 141)
Semantics is the study of meaning in language. There is more interest in certain aspects of meaning
than in others. There are different types of meanings. We can have the following types of meaning:
   ❖ Lexical meaning refers to the meaning of words that belong to one of the four lexical word
     classes. It is the aspect of meaning usually given in a dictionary.
   ❖ Grammatical meaning includes the meaning of grammatical items (e.g., function words
     and inflectional affixes), grammatical functions (e.g., subject and object), and different
     sentence-types (e.g., declarative and interrogative). Taking into account certain non-

   ❖ Referential meaning (also called denotative meaning, descriptive meaning, conceptual
     meaning, or sense) refers to the logical, cognitive, or denotative content of an expression.
   ❖ Connotative meaning (associative meaning) denotes the associations and secondary
     meanings the expression evokes.
   ❖ Social meaning (stylistic meaning) is the information that the linguistic expression
     conveys about certain social characteristics.
   ❖ Emotive or affective component of the expression is referred to as its affective meaning.
     Social meaning and affective meaning together are sometimes called connotation.
   ❖ Reflected meaning refers to certain associations with another sense of the same
     expression, whereas collocative meaning (collocation) is conveyed by characteristic word
     combinations.
   ❖ Thematic meaning denotes the organization of a message in terms of information
     structure.
Q. briefly explain Denotative meaning (Topic 142)
Conceptual meaning or denotative meaning covers those basic, essential components of meaning
that are conveyed by the literal use of a word. It is the type of meaning that dictionaries are
designed to describe. Some of the basic components of a word like ‘needle’ in English might
include “thin, sharp, steel instrument.” These components would be part of the conceptual meaning

WHILE ANIMALS POSSESS REMARKABLE INTELLIGENCE AND
SENSITIVITIES, THEIR COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS DIFFER
SIGNIFICANTLY FROM HUMAN LANGUAGE. ANIMAL
COMMUNICATION SERVES PRIMARILY TO CONVEY EMOTIONS,
ALERT TO DANGERS, AND MAINTAIN SOCIAL COHESION WITHIN
THEIR GROUPS. IT LACKS THE KEY CHARACTERISTICS THAT
DEFINE LANGUAGE, SUCH AS:

  1. **ARBITRARINESS:** ANIMAL SIGNALS ARE DIRECTLY
     LINKED TO THE EMOTIONS OR SITUATIONS THEY REPRESENT,
     UNLIKE HUMAN LANGUAGE, WHERE WORDS AND SYMBOLS
     ARE ARBITRARILY ASSIGNED TO MEANINGS.

  2. **PRODUCTIVITY:** ANIMALS CANNOT COMBINE SIGNALS IN
     NEW WAYS TO FORM NOVEL EXPRESSIONS, UNLIKE HUMANS
     WHO CAN CREATE AN INFINITE NUMBER OF SENTENCES
     USING A FINITE SET OF WORDS.

  3. **DISPLACEMENT:** ANIMALS CANNOT REFER TO THINGS OR
     EVENTS THAT ARE NOT PHYSICALLY PRESENT, UNLIKE
     HUMANS WHO CAN DISCUSS THE PAST, PRESENT, OR FUTURE.

  4. **DUALITY:** ANIMAL COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS DO NOT
     HAVE DISTINCT LEVELS OF MEANING, SUCH AS THE
     COMBINATION OF SOUNDS (PHONEMES) TO FORM WORDS
     (MORPHEMES) AND WORDS TO FORM SENTENCES (GRAMMAR),
     AS SEEN IN HUMAN LANGUAGE.

  5. **OPENNESS:** ANIMAL COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS ARE

﻿
A foreign language can have both positive and negative impacts on the culture, identity, and society of a nation.
On one hand, the adoption and flourishing of a foreign language can bring benefits. It can enhance communication and facilitate global interactions, enabling cultural exchange and economic opportunities. Learning a foreign language can broaden perspectives, foster understanding between nations, and promote cultural diversity. It can also empower individuals to engage with different cultures and appreciate their values and traditions, leading to a more inclusive and interconnected society.
On the other hand, the dominance of a foreign language can pose challenges. It may lead to the erosion of indigenous languages and the loss of cultural heritage. Language is intricately connected to identity, and when a foreign language becomes prevalent, it can diminish the sense of belonging and pride in one's own culture. Moreover, language barriers can create divisions within society, hindering social integration and exacerbating inequalities. In some cases, the imposition of a foreign language can be a tool of cultural assimilation, suppressing local languages, traditions, and customs.
In summary, the impact of a foreign language on a nation's culture, identity, and society is complex. While it can bring advantages such as global connectivity and cultural exchange, it can also lead to the erosion of local languages and cultural traditions. Striking a balance between embracing foreign languages and preserving indigenous languages is crucial to maintaining cultural diversity and fostering a harmonious society.

Animals have their own intelligence and sensitivities. Animals possess distinct intelligence and
sensitivities, showcasing unique communication methods. Exploring these characteristics reveals
a fascinating array of signals, including vocalizations, body movements, facial expressions, and
chemical cues. These signals convey vital information like warnings, mating calls, or territorial
boundaries among animals.
Despite these sophisticated communication systems, differences exist between animal
communication and human language. Animal communication tends to be more limited and
instinctual, lacking the complexity and flexibility inherent in human language. While animals
effectively communicate within their species, their systems lack the versatility of human
language.
Moreover, animal communication is often triggered by specific stimuli, unlike human language,
which enables abstract concept expression, emotional communication, and complex
conversations. The property of displacement, allowing discussion of non-present elements, is a
unique feature of human language absent in animal communication.
Recognizing the sophistication of animal communication, it's crucial to acknowledge its
distinctions from human language. Although animals communicate effectively within their
species, the complexity of human language sets it apart. Understanding these differences
enhances appreciation for the diverse ways species interact and share information.

ENG502_Glossary

 1. Affective Meaning :The emotive or affective component of the expression is
    referred to as its affective meaning. Social meaning and affective meaning
    together are sometimes called connotation.
 2. Agent :Agent is the semantic role of a person or thing who is the doer of an
    event.
 3. Anaphora :The use of a word referring back to a word used earlier in a text
    or conversation, to avoid repetition, for example the pronouns he, she, it, and
    they and the verb do.
 4. Anaphoric Expression :Anaphora can be defined as a subsequent reference
    to an already introduced entity.
 5. Antonymy :Two forms with opposite meanings are called antonyms.
 6. Aphasia :Aphasia is defined as an impairment of language function due to
    localized brain damage that leads to difficulty in understanding and/or
    producing linguistic forms.
 7. Applied Linguistics :Applied linguistics is an interdisciplinary field of
    linguistics which identifies, investigates, and offers solutions to language-
    related real-life problems.
 8. Arbitrariness :In human language, there is no natural connection between the
    word and the object they make reference to. This characteristic of language is
    called arbitrariness. For example, the Arabic word ‘kalab’ meaning dog and
    the English word ‘dog’ have no relation to the word they refer to.
 9. Benefactive :The entity that benefits from the action or event denoted by the
    predicate.
 10.         Bilingualism :Bilingualism: the ability of an individual or the members
    of a community to use two languages effectively.

By ASFAND YARR

                          ENG502_Glossary

 11.     Binaural :It is binaural reception when somebody speaks. The listener
   knows where the speaker is. This is the characteristic which is in both human
   beings as well as animals.
 12.     Chronemics :In communication, chronemics means the study of how
   time affects communication and includes how different time cycles affect our
   communication.
 13.     Coherence :Coherence refers to the quality of being logical and
   consistent, e.g., 'This essay, on the whole, lacks coherence'.
 14.     Cohesion :Cohesion is the grammatical and lexical linking within a text
   or sentence that holds a text together and gives it meaning.
 15.     Computational Linguistics :Computational linguistics is the branch of
   linguistics in which the techniques of computer science are applied to the
   analysis and synthesis of language and speech.
 16.     Conceptual Meaning :Conceptual meaning is the clear and logical
   definition of a word based on the structure and form of the word An example
   of conceptual meaning would be the word ‘cat’.
 17.     Connotation :Connotation represents the various social overtones,
   cultural implications, or emotional meanings associated with a sign.
 18.     Contrastive Linguistics :Contrastive linguistics: a practice-oriented
   linguistic approach that seeks to describe the differences and similarities
   between a pair of languages.
 19.     Conversation :Conversation is interactive communication between
   two or more people.

By ASFAND YARR

                           ENG502_Glossary

 20.      Conversation Analysis :Conversation analysis (CA) is an approach to
   the study of social interaction, embracing both verbal and non-verbal conduct,
   in situations of everyday life.
 21.      Creole :When a pidgin develops beyond its role as a trade or contact
   language and becomes the first language of a social community, it is described
   as a creole.
 22.      Critical Discourse Analysis :Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) has
   roots in both Discourse Analysis (DA) and Critical Linguistics (CL). It is an
   interdisciplinary method to investigating discourses and language within
   public institutions laid out by Norman Fairclough in his book “Language and
   Power”.
 23.      Critical Social Theory :Critical Social Theory (CST) provides a
   theoretical foundation for critical approaches to discourse analysis.
 24.      Cultural Transmission :Language is acquired in a culture with other
   speakers and not from parental genes. This property of human language is
   cultural transmission wherein a language is passed on from one generation to
   the next within a cultural setting.
 25.      Deixis/Deictic expression :A deictic expression (or deixis) is a word
   or phrase (such as this, that, these, those, now, then) that points to the time,
   place, or situation in which a speaker is speaking.
 26.      Denotation :Denotation represents the explicit or referential meaning
   of a sign.
 27.      Derivational Morphemes :In morphology, derivational morphemes
   show the “inner” layer of words and they are attached to the stem.

By ASFAND YARR

                            ENG502_Glossary

 28.      Dialect :Dialect is a particular form of a language which is peculiar to
   a specific region or social group.
 29.      Diglossia :A situation in which two distinct varieties of a language are
   spoken within the same speech community.
 30.      Discourse :A unit of language which can be less or more than one
   sentence but has a meaning beyond the level of sentence.
 31.      Discourse Analysis :Discourse Analysis (DA), or discourse studies, is
   a general term for a number of approaches to analyze written, vocal, or sign
   language use, or any significant semiotic event.
 32.      Discreteness :The sounds used in language are meaningfully distinct,
   i.e., each sound in the language is treated as discrete, for example, / l/, /i:/, and
   /n/. We can join them to make a word 'lean' transcribed as / li:n / or if we
   change the order, we get another word 'kneel' transcribed as /ni:l/.
 33.      Displacement :In linguistics, displacement is the capability of
   language to communicate about things that are not immediately present
   (spatially or temporally); i.e., things that are either not here or are not here
   now.
 34.      Duality :Human language is organized at two levels or layers

ENG502
➡️ Language: A Purely Human and Non-Instinctive Communication

Language is a unique and complex system of communication exclusive to humans. Unlike
animals, humans possess the ability to create and understand complex linguistic structures,
enabling us to convey thoughts, emotions, and ideas. This capacity for language is not innate but
learned through experience and interaction.

➡️ Language: A Symbol System

Language operates as a symbol system, where sounds, words, and gestures represent concepts,
objects, and ideas. These symbols hold arbitrary meanings agreed upon by language users. The
English language, for instance, uses a combination of alphabets, phonemes, and morphemes to
convey meaning.

➡️ Behavioristic View of Language

The behavioristic perspective views language as a learned behavior shaped by environment,
experience, and reinforcement. This theory suggests that language acquisition occurs through
interaction with others, imitation, and conditioning. In English language learning, behavioristic
approaches emphasize repetition, drill, and practice.

➡️ Structural View of Language

The structural perspective examines language's internal structure, comprising sounds
(phonology), words (morphology), sentences (syntax), and meaning (semantics). English
language's structural components, such as verb tenses and clause structures, work together to
convey meaning.

➡️ Miscellaneous Definitions of Language

Language definitions vary, including system of signs and symbols, tool for communication,
expression of thought and feeling, and social construct. These perspectives highlight language's
multifaceted nature, emphasizing its role in shaping identity, culture, and society.

➡️ History of Language

Language has evolved over time, influenced by geographical, cultural, and social factors. English
language's history, for example, spans Old English, Middle English, and Modern English,
reflecting the impact of Norman Conquest, Renaissance, and colonialism.

➡️ Animal Communication and Language

Animal communication differs significantly from human language. While animals use
vocalizations, gestures, and chemical signals, their systems lack the complexity, creativity, and
symbolic nature of human language.

➡️ Talking Apes

Studies on talking apes, such as chimpanzees and bonobos, demonstrate their capacity for
language acquisition. However, their linguistic abilities differ fundamentally from humans',
highlighting the unique characteristics of human language.

➡️ Written Language

Written language emerged around 5,000 years ago, revolutionizing communication and
knowledge transmission. English language's written form has evolved from runes to modern
alphabets.

➡️ First Families

Language families, such as Indo-European and Sino-Tibetan, group languages based on shared
ancestry. English belongs to the Germanic branch of Indo-European languages.

➡️ Towards a Science of Language

Linguistics, the scientific study of language, seeks to understand language's structure, evolution,
and use. English language linguistics examines phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, and
semantics.

➡️ Origin of Language

Theories on language origin include:

   -   The Divine Source: Language as a gift from God.
   -   The Natural Sound Source: Language emerging from natural sounds.
   -   The Social Interaction Source: Language developing through human interaction.
   -   The Physical Adaptation Source: Language adapting to physical environment.
   -   The Tool-Making Source: Language emerging with tool use.
   -   The Genetic Source: Language influenced by genetics.

➡️ Characteristics of Human Language

   -   Displacement: Language can refer to past, present, or future.
   -   Arbitrariness: Words have no inherent meaning.
   -   Productivity: Language allows creativity.
   -   Cultural Transmission: Language passed through culture.
   -   Duality: Language consists of sounds and meaning.

➡️ Functions of Language (Verbal Communication)

Language serves various purposes, including expression, persuasion, control, and performance.
Verbal communication facilitates information exchange, relationship building, and social
interaction.

➡️ Language is Expressive

Language enables users to convey thoughts, emotions, and experiences. Through vocabulary,
tone, and syntax, speakers express themselves, shaping their identity and relationships.

➡️ Language is Powerful

Language influences others, shaping perceptions and actions. Powerful language can inspire,
persuade, or manipulate, highlighting its impact on social dynamics.

➡️ Language as a Means of Control

Language regulates behavior, enforcing social norms and expectations. Authority figures use
language to direct, command, or prohibit actions.

➡️ Language is Performative

Language accomplishes actions, such as promising, apologizing, or congratulating. Performative
language has real-world consequences.

➡️ Language: A Dynamic and Relational Entity

Language constantly evolves, influenced by context, culture, and interaction. Its relational nature
connects individuals, groups, and societies.

➡️ NONVERBAL COMMUNICATION

Nonverbal cues convey information beyond verbal language.

➡️ Aspects of Nonverbal Communication

Nonverbal communication involves:

   -   Facial expressions
   -   Body language
   -   Eye contact
   -   Touch
   -   Proximity
   -   Tone and pitch

➡️ Principles of Nonverbal Communication

Effective nonverbal communication relies on:

   -   Consistency
   -   Congruence
   -   Contextualization

Conveyance of Interpersonal and Emotional Messages

Nonverbal cues convey emotions, attitudes, and relationships.

More Involuntary than Verbal

Nonverbal communication often occurs unconsciously.

More Ambiguous

Nonverbal cues can be open to interpretation.

More Credible

Nonverbal communication can be more trustworthy than verbal language.

➡️ Types of Nonverbal Communication

   -   Kinesics (body language)
   -   Haptics (touch)
   -   Vocalics (tone/pitch)

 Q. Allograph

    1. a letter of an alphabet in a particular shape (such as A or a) A variant shape of a letter
    2. any of the ways a unit of a writing system, as the letter of an alphabet, is formed or shaped
    3. any of the units or combinations of unit that can represent one phoneme as /f/
    4. Writing especially a signature, made by one person for another. So, we can see that
       allograph is the opposite of autograph.

 Q. What is the functional morpheme?

 A functional morpheme simply modifies the meaning of the word, rather than supplying the
 root meaning of the word. It encodes grammatical meaning e.g., the girls entered the classroom.
 In this sentence, ‘the’ is functional morpheme, which is specifying girl and classroom.
 Functional morphemes belong to the ‘closed’ class of words. Normally, new functional
 morphemes cannot be coined.

 Q. discuss traditional grammar

 Traditional Grammar          The terms ‘article,’, ‘adjective’, and ‘noun’ that we use to label the
 grammatical categories of the words in the phrase the lucky boys come from traditional
 grammar, which has its origins in the description of languages such as Latin and Greek. Since
 there were well-established grammatical descriptions of these languages, it seemed appropriate
 to adopt the existing categories from these descriptions and apply them in the analysis of
 ‘newer’ languages such as English. The best-known terms from that tradition are those used in
 describing the parts of speech.
 Q. types of stress
 The stress placed on words within sentences is called sentence stress or prosodic stress. The
 stress tells the listener which words are important. Most unstressed words are ignored or
 discarded. it is difficult to define stress solely phonetically.
 In English there are three types of stress:

    ▪   syllable stress. when one syllable in a word is pronounced louder and more clearly than
        adjacent syllables.
     ▪ word stress. when one word is pronounced louder and more clearly than adjacent words
        in a sentence.
     ▪ phrase, clause or sentence stress.
 Q. Language is a mean of control
 Controlled languages (sometimes called controlled natural languages or CNLs) are subsets of
 human languages, such as English or Chinese. Controlled languages use restricted grammar
 rules and vocabularies (typically between 800 and 1,000 words) to reduce or eliminate

 Q. Social interaction source Language is the foundation for most social interaction.
 People use language to acquire goods, services, and information and to make public their
 thoughts and feelings. They use language in informal encounters with friends and family and in
 more task-oriented or highly scripted encounters, such as those occurring in school and the
 workplace. They also use language in face-to-face encounters as well as in encounters with
 partners who are not visible to them, such as when they speak on the telephone.
 Q. Define monosyllable, disyllable, Bisyllable, Trisyllable and Polysyllable.
 A word that consists of a single syllable (speech sound) (like English dog) is called a
 monosyllable (and is said to be monosyllabic). Similar terms include disyllable and disyllabic
 (also bisyllable and bisyllabic) for a word of two syllables; trisyllable (and trisyllabic) for a
 word of three syllables; and polysyllable (and polysyllabic), which may refer either to a word
 of more than three syllables or to any word of more than one syllable. An ideal syllable consists
 of CVC (Consonant Vowel Consonant), for example, cat/kæt/. However, there can be variety in
 the structure of the syllable.

 Interchangeability refers to the idea that humans can give and receive identical linguistic
 signals; humans are not limited in the types of messages they can say/hear. One can say "I am
 a boy" even if one is a girl. This is not to be confused with lying (prevarication). The importance
 is that a speaker can physically create any and all messages regardless of their truth or relation
 to the speaker. In other words, anything that one can hear, one can also say. Interchangeability
 refers to the speaker’s ability to both receive and broadcast the same signal. This is different to
 some communication systems where, for example, males produce one set of behaviours and
 females another and they are unable to interchange these messages so that males use the female
 signal and vice versa.

 The word grammar is from Greek word which means "art of letters", (gramma), "letter".
 Grammar is the set of structural rules governing the composition of clauses, phrases, and words
 in any given natural language. The term refers also to the study of such rules, and this field
 includes phonology, morphology, and syntax, often complemented by phonetics, semantics, and
 pragmatics.

see a sentence like “To boldly go where no man has gone before” and would try to describe how the mental
grammar can cause that ordering of words, rather than saying that the surface form is faulty due to prescriptive rules
(which would require the sentence “To go boldly where no man has gone before”). Linguistics takes this approach to
language.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN PRESCRIPTIVE LINGUISTICS and DESCRIPTIVE LINGUISTICS

Prescriptive grammar describes when people focus on talking about how a language should or ought to be used. One
way to remember this association is to think of going to a doctor’s office. When a doctor gives you a prescription for
medication, it often includes directions about how you should take your medication as well as what you should not
do when taking your medication. In a similar way, a prescriptive grammar tells you how you should speak, and what
type of language to avoid. This is commonly found in English classes as well as other language classes, where the
aim is to teach people how to use language in a very particular (typically described as ‘proper’ or ‘correct’) way.
Descriptive grammar, on the other hand, focuses on describing the language as it is used, not saying how it should
be used. For example, think about a prescriptive rule like Don’t split infinitives. A descriptive grammarian would
see a sentence like “To boldly go where no man has gone before” and would try to describe how the mental
grammar can cause that ordering of words, rather than saying that the surface form is faulty due to prescriptive rules
(which would require the sentence “To go boldly where no man has gone before”). Linguistics takes this approach to
language.

1. When nouns and adjectives possess two syllables the stress is on the first syllable. Examples: PRO-gress

2. Verbs possess two syllables the stress is on the last syllable. Examples: pre-SENT

Example: e-du-CA-tion

4. Words ending on –IC are usually stressed on second last syllable. Examples: e-co-NO-mic

5. Words ending in –EE and –OO are usually stressed on last syllable. Example: em-poly-EE

Non-Speculative Nature Linguistics is non-speculative. So the main difference between scientific and non-scientific
study of language is that linguistics is empirical rather than speculative or intuitive. It operates with publically
verifiable data obtained by means of observation and experiment. Speculative mood (abbreviated spec) is an
epistemic grammatical mood found in some languages, which indicates that the utterance is based on speculation of
the speaker, and not necessarily known to be the case. For example, "The butler could have been the killer."

Q. What is the functional morpheme?

A functional morpheme simply modifies the meaning of the word, rather than supplying the root meaning of the
word. It encodes grammatical meaning e.g., the girls entered the classroom. In this sentence, ‘the’ is functional
morpheme, which is specifying girl and classroom. Functional morphemes belong to the ‘closed’ class of words.
Normally, new functional morphemes cannot be coined.

Q. discuss traditional grammar

Traditional Grammar The terms ‘article,’, ‘adjective’, and ‘noun’ that we use to label the grammatical categories
of the words in the phrase the lucky boys come from traditional grammar, which has its origins in the description of
languages such as Latin and Greek. Since there were well-established grammatical descriptions of these languages,
it seemed appropriate to adopt the existing categories from these descriptions and apply them in the analysis of
‘newer’ languages such as English. The best-known terms from that tradition are those used in describing the parts
of speech.

Q. types of stress

The stress placed on words within sentences is called sentence stress or prosodic stress. The stress tells the listener
which words are important. Most unstressed words are ignored or discarded. it is difficult to define stress solely
phonetically.

In English there are three types of stress:

        syllable stress. when one syllable in a word is pronounced louder and more clearly than adjacent syllables.
        word stress. when one word is pronounced louder and more clearly than adjacent words in a sentence.
        phrase, clause or sentence stress.

Q. Language is a mean of control

Controlled languages (sometimes called controlled natural languages or CNLs) are subsets of human languages,
such as English or Chinese. Controlled languages use restricted grammar rules and vocabularies (typically between
800 and 1,000 words) to reduce or eliminate ambiguity and complexity.

Q. Define monosyllable, disyllable, Bisyllable, Trisyllable and Polysyllable.

A word that consists of a single syllable (speech sound) (like English dog) is called a monosyllable (and is said to be
monosyllabic). Similar terms include disyllable and disyllabic (also bisyllable and bisyllabic) for a word of two
syllables; trisyllable (and trisyllabic) for a word of three syllables; and polysyllable (and polysyllabic), which may
refer either to a word of more than three syllables or to any word of more than one syllable. An ideal syllable
consists of CVC (Consonant Vowel Consonant), for example, cat/kæt/. However, there can be variety in the
structure of the syllable.

Q. Interchangeability write examples

Interchangeability refers to the idea that humans can give and receive identical linguistic signals; humans are not
limited in the types of messages they can say/hear. One can say "I am a boy" even if one is a girl. This is not to be
confused with lying (prevarication). The importance is that a speaker can physically create any and all messages
regardless of their truth or relation to the speaker. In other words, anything that one can hear, one can also say.
Interchangeability refers to the speaker’s ability to both receive and broadcast the same signal. This is different to
some communication systems where, for example, males produce one set of behaviours and females another and
they are unable to interchange these messages so that males use the female signal and vice versa.

Q. WHAT IS GRAMMAR?

The word grammar is from Greek word which means "art of letters", (gramma), "letter". Grammar is the set of
structural rules governing the composition of clauses, phrases, and words in any given natural language. The term
refers also to the study of such rules, and this field includes phonology, morphology, and syntax, often
complemented by phonetics, semantics, and pragmatics.

Grammar refers to cognitive information underlying language use. Speakers of a language have a set of internalized
rules for using that language. These rules constitute grammar, and the vast majority of the information in the
grammar is—at least in the case of one's native language—acquired not by conscious study or instruction, but by
observing other speakers.

Interchangeability write examples

Interchangeability refers to the idea that humans can give and receive identical linguistic signals; humans are not
limited in the types of messages they can say/hear. One can say "I am a boy" even if one is a girl. This is not to be
confused with lying (prevarication). The importance is that a speaker can physically create any and all messages
regardless of their truth or relation to the speaker. In other words, anything that one can hear, one can also say.
Interchangeability refers to the speaker’s ability to both receive and broadcast the same signal. This is different to
some communication systems where, for example, males produce one set of behaviours and females another and
they are unable to interchange these messages so that males use the female signal and vice versa.

IMP: WHAT IS GRAMMAR?

The word grammar is from Greek word which means "art of letters", (gramma), "letter". Grammar is the set of
structural rules governing the composition of clauses, phrases, and words in any given natural language. The term
refers also to the study of such rules, and this field includes phonology, morphology, and syntax, often
complemented by phonetics, semantics, and pragmatics.

Grammar refers to cognitive information underlying language use. Speakers of a language have a set of internalized
rules for using that language. These rules constitute grammar, and the vast majority of the information in the
grammar is—at least in the case of one's native language—acquired not by conscious study or instruction, but by
observing other speakers. Much of this work is done during early childhood; learning a language later in life usually
involves a greater degree of explicit instruction English has strict rules for combining words into phrases.

• Verb Phrase

If the first syllable of a word begins with a vowel, it can be any vowel except /ʊ/ which is rare. Initial consonant of a

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN PRESCRIPTIVE LINGUISTICS and DESCRIPTIVE LINGUISTICS

Prescriptive grammar describes when people focus on talking about how a language should or ought to be used. One
way to remember this association is to think of going to a doctor’s office. When a doctor gives you a prescription for
medication, it often includes directions about how you should take your medication as well as what you should not
do when taking your medication. In a similar way, a prescriptive grammar tells you how you should speak, and what
type of language to avoid. This is commonly found in English classes as well as other language classes, where the
aim is to teach people how to use language in a very particular (typically described as ‘proper’ or ‘correct’) way.
Descriptive grammar, on the other hand, focuses on describing the language as it is used, not saying how it should
be used. For example, think about a prescriptive rule like Don’t split infinitives. A descriptive grammarian would
see a sentence like “To boldly go where no man has gone before” and would try to describe how the mental
grammar can cause that ordering of words, rather than saying that the surface form is faulty due to prescriptive rules
(which would require the sentence “To go boldly where no man has gone before”). Linguistics takes this approach to
language.

Q. Allograph

    1.   a letter of an alphabet in a particular shape (such as A or a) A variant shape of a letter
    2.   any of the ways a unit of a writing system, as the letter of an alphabet, is formed or shaped
    3.   any of the units or combinations of unit that can represent one phoneme as /f/
    4.   Writing especially a signature, made by one person for another. So, we can see that allograph is the
         opposite of autograph.

Q. What is the functional morpheme?

A functional morpheme simply modifies the meaning of the word, rather than supplying the root meaning of the
word. It encodes grammatical meaning e.g., the girls entered the classroom. In this sentence, ‘the’ is functional
morpheme, which is specifying girl and classroom. Functional morphemes belong to the ‘closed’ class of words.
Normally, new functional morphemes cannot be coined.

Q. discuss traditional grammar

Traditional Grammar The terms ‘article,’, ‘adjective’, and ‘noun’ that we use to label the grammatical categories
of the words in the phrase the lucky boys come from traditional grammar, which has its origins in the description of
languages such as Latin and Greek. Since there were well-established grammatical descriptions of these languages,
it seemed appropriate to adopt the existing categories from these descriptions and apply them in the analysis of
‘newer’ languages such as English. The best-known terms from that tradition are those used in describing the parts
of speech.

Q. types of stress

The stress placed on words within sentences is called sentence stress or prosodic stress. The stress tells the listener
which words are important. Most unstressed words are ignored or discarded. it is difficult to define stress solely
phonetically.

In English there are three types of stress:

        syllable stress. when one syllable in a word is pronounced louder and more clearly than adjacent syllables.
        word stress. when one word is pronounced louder and more clearly than adjacent words in a sentence.
        phrase, clause or sentence stress.

Q. Language is a mean of control

Controlled languages (sometimes called controlled natural languages or CNLs) are subsets of human languages,
such as English or Chinese. Controlled languages use restricted grammar rules and vocabularies (typically between
800 and 1,000 words) to reduce or eliminate ambiguity and complexity.

Q. Social interaction source Language is the foundation for most social interaction.

People use language to acquire goods, services, and information and to make public their thoughts and feelings.
They use language in informal encounters with friends and family and in more task-oriented or highly scripted

Q. Define monosyllable, disyllable, Bisyllable, Trisyllable and Polysyllable.

A word that consists of a single syllable (speech sound) (like English dog) is called a monosyllable (and is said to be
monosyllabic). Similar terms include disyllable and disyllabic (also bisyllable and bisyllabic) for a word of two
syllables; trisyllable (and trisyllabic) for a word of three syllables; and polysyllable (and polysyllabic), which may
refer either to a word of more than three syllables or to any word of more than one syllable. An ideal syllable
consists of CVC (Consonant Vowel Consonant), for example, cat/kæt/. However, there can be variety in the
structure of the syllable.

monosyllabic). Similar terms include disyllable and disyllabic (also bisyllable and bisyllabic) for a word of two
syllables; trisyllable (and trisyllabic) for a word of three syllables; and polysyllable (and polysyllabic), which may
refer either to a word of more than three syllables or to any word of more than one syllable. An ideal syllable
consists of CVC (Consonant Vowel Consonant), for example, cat/kæt/. However, there can be variety in the
structure of the syllable.

Q. Interchangeability write examples

Interchangeability refers to the idea that humans can give and receive identical linguistic signals; humans are not
limited in the types of messages they can say/hear. One can say "I am a boy" even if one is a girl. This is not to be
confused with lying (prevarication). The importance is that a speaker can physically create any and all messages
regardless of their truth or relation to the speaker. In other words, anything that one can hear, one can also say.
Interchangeability refers to the speaker’s ability to both receive and broadcast the same signal. This is different to
some communication systems where, for example, males produce one set of behaviours and females another and
they are unable to interchange these messages so that males use the female signal and vice versa.

Q. WHAT IS GRAMMAR?

The word grammar is from Greek word which means "art of letters", (gramma), "letter". Grammar is the set of
structural rules governing the composition of clauses, phrases, and words in any given natural language. The term
refers also to the study of such rules, and this field includes phonology, morphology, and syntax, often
complemented by phonetics, semantics, and pragmatics.

Grammar refers to cognitive information underlying language use. Speakers of a language have a set of internalized
rules for using that language. These rules constitute grammar, and the vast majority of the information in the
grammar is—at least in the case of one's native language—acquired not by conscious study or instruction, but by
observing other speakers.

Q. Zero Onset:

If the first syllable of a word begins with a vowel, it can be any vowel except /ʊ/ which is rare. Initial consonant of a
word may be any except /ŋ/.

Prescriptive grammar describes when people focus on talking about how a language should or ought to be used. One
way to remember this association is to think of going to a doctor’s office. When a doctor gives you a prescription for

Q. E-Dictionary:

An electronic dictionary is a dictionary whose data exists in digital form and can be accessed
through a number of different media.

Electronic dictionaries can be found in several forms, including:

   as dedicated handheld devices

  as apps on smartphones and tablet computers or computer software

  as a function built into an E-reader

As CD-ROMs and DVD-ROMs, they are typically packaged with a printed dictionary to be
installed on the user’s own computer. As free or paid-for online products most of the early
electronic dictionaries were print dictionaries made available in digital form. The content was
identical. But the electronic editions provided users with more powerful search functions. But
soon the opportunities offered by digital media began to be exploited.

Electronic dictionary databases, especially those included with software dictionaries are often
extensive and can contain up to 500,000 headwords and definitions, verb conjugation tables, and

a grammar reference section. Bilingual electronic dictionaries and monolingual dictionaries of
inflected languages often include an interactive verb conjugator, and are capable of word
stemming and lemmatization. Electronic dictionaries are also available in logographic and right-
to-left scripts, including Arabic, Persian, Chinese, Devanagari, Greek, Hebrew, Japanese,
Korean, and Thai. Several developers of the systems that drive electronic dictionary software
offer API and SDK – Software Development Kit tools for adding various language-based
functions to programs, and web services such as the AJAX API used by Google.

Q. Two Phrase Structure Rule:

These are the rules that form phrases of different types e.g., noun phrase, verb phrase, and
adjective phrase etc. A tree diagram can have two different ways: simply as a static
representation of the structure of the sentence shown at the bottom of the tree diagram. Every
single sentence can have a tree diagram. The other one is the dynamic format which is a way of
generating not only that particular sentence, but a very large number of other sentences with
similar structures. This second approach is very appealing because it would enable us to generate
a very large number of sentences with what looks like a very small number of rules. These rules
are called phrase structure rules.

PAID VU LMS HANDLING by Mam Mehwish
                 03184148783
 Past Papers for Mids./Finals are also Available

1. Nonverbal communication doesn’t have____________________ rules of
grammar that bring structure, order, and agreed-on patterns of usage.
 - Options: a) formalexplicit b) implicit c) ambiguous
 - Correct Answer: c) ambiguous

2. A lack of nonverbal communication competence related to touch could have
negative interpersonal consequences.
 - Options: a) False b) True
 - Correct Answer: b) True

3. All languages require the organizing and combining of sounds
of____________in specific arrangements.
 - Options: a) symptoms b) signposts c) signs d) trails
 - Correct Answer: c) signs

4. The involuntary or subconscious nature of ____________________
communication makes it less easy to fake, which makes it seem more honest and
credible.
 - Options: a) verbatim b) nonverbal c) structural d) verbal
 - Correct Answer: b) nonverbal

5. Para-language includes _____.
 - Options: a) gestures b) volume c) eye-contact d) expressions
 - Correct Answer: b) volume

6. Words and phrases tell who we are and contribute to the ______ that others
make of us.
 - Options: a) expressions b) imitation c) impressions d) effects
 - Correct Answer: c) impressions

7. The variety of ____________________ increases listener and speaker
engagement, understanding, information recall, and motivation.
 - Options: a) haptics b) proxemics c) vocalics d) chronemics
 - Correct Answer: c) vocalics

8. "Humans are continually creating new expressions and novel utterances by using
their linguistic resources to describe new objects and situations" is called ______.
  - Options: a) productivity b) arbitrariness c) displacement d) cultural
transmission
 - Correct Answer: a) productivity

9. In legal contexts, ______ language can be a means of control.
 - Options: a) considerate b) performative c) courteous d) dynamic
 - Correct Answer: b) performative

10. Teeth, lips, mouth, larynx, and pharynx are the examples
of_________________.

   - Options: a) physical adaptation sources b) None of the above given options c)
instrumental adaptation sources d) artificial adaptation sources
  - Correct Answer: a) physical adaptation sources

. 1.stress timed

WHAT IS LANGUAGE?: Language is a system of communication that consists of a set
of rules and symbols used to convey meaning and express thoughts, ideas, and experiences.
It is a fundamental aspect of human society, enabling us to interact, share knowledge, and
build relationships.
Language: A Purely Human and Non-Instinctive: Language is a unique and exclusive
attribute of humans, distinguishing us from animals. It is a learned skill, not an innate
ability, and is shaped by culture, history, and social context. Human language is complex,
creative, and symbolic, setting it apart from other forms of communication.
Communication: Language is a unique characteristic of humans, unlike animal
communication, which is largely instinctive. Human language is learned, not innate, and is
shaped by culture, environment, and social context.
Language: A Symbol System: Language uses symbols, such as words, sounds, and
gestures, to represent concepts, objects, and ideas. These symbols are arbitrary, meaning
their meaning is not inherent but agreed upon by the language community.
Behavioristic View of Language: The behavioristic view sees language as a behavior
shaped by environment, conditioning, and reinforcement. It emphasizes the role of
imitation, habit, and association in language learning and use.
Structural View of Language: The structural view, developed by linguist Ferdinand de
Saussure, sees language as a system of signs with underlying rules and structures. It
analyzes language as a network of relationships between signs and their meanings.
Miscellaneous Definitions of Language: Language has been defined in various ways,
such as a tool for communication, a means of expression, a system of signs, a social
construct, and a reflection of culture and thought.
HISTORY OF LANGUAGE: The history of language is long and complex, spanning
millions of years. It is believed to have originated from gestures, sounds, and facial
expressions, evolving into complex systems of communication.
Animal Communication and Language: Animals communicate using various signals,
such as sounds, gestures, and body language. While they do not possess language in the
human sense, their communication systems share some similarities with human language.

       Talking Apes: Some primates, like chimpanzees and gorillas, have been taught human
       sign language, demonstrating an ability to learn and use language symbols.
       Written Language: Written language developed around 5,000 years ago, allowing for the
       recording and transmission of language across time and space.
       First Families: The first language families, such as Indo-European and Sino-Tibetan,
       emerged around 6,000-8,000 years ago, spreading across continents and giving rise to
       many modern languages.
       Towards a Science of Language: The study of language has evolved into a scientific
       discipline, incorporating insights from linguistics, psychology, anthropology, and
       computer science to understand the nature, structure, and use of language.
       Future Indicatives: The future of language is shaped by technological advancements,
       globalization, and evolving human communication needs, likely leading to new forms of
       language, such as digital and virtual communication systems.
       The Divine Source: language as a gift from God or gods
       The Natural Sound Source: language emerging from natural sounds and gestures
       The Social Interaction Source: language developing through social interaction and
       communication needs
       The Physical Adaptation Source:
Language may have originated from physical adaptations such as:
                Gestures and body language
                Facial expressions and emotions
                Vocalizations and sound-making abilities
       The Tool-Making Source
Language may have emerged as a result of tool-making and:

                 Cognitive abilities to create and use tools
                 Need for communication to coordinate tool-making activities
                 Development of symbolic thinking and representation
       The Genetic Source:
                 Inherent abilities for language acquisition and use
                 Evolutionary advantages for language development
                 Genetic predispositions for language structure and organization
       Characteristics of Human Language
                Displacement
                Arbitrariness
                Productivity
                Cultural Transmission
                Duality
       Displacement: language allows us to communicate about things not present

Arbitrariness: language symbols have no inherent meaning
Productivity: language enables us to create new expressions and meanings
Cultural Transmission: language is passed down through culture and society
Duality: language has both a tangible (sound, writing) and intangible (meaning, thought)
aspect
Functions of Language
         Language is Expressive: Language allows us to express thoughts, feelings, and
            ideas (e.g., "I'm so happy to see you!").
         Language is Powerful: Language can influence others, shape opinions, and
            assert control (e.g., political speeches).
         Language is Performative: Language can perform actions, make promises, and
            create commitments (e.g., "I promise to meet you at 5 pm").
NONVERBAL COMMUNICATION AND LINGUISTICS
        Aspects of Nonverbal Communication: (Facial expressions, body language, tone
           of voice, and eye contact convey meaning beyond spoken language.)
        Principles of Nonverbal Communication: Nonverbal cues can reinforce,
           contradict, or complement verbal messages (e.g., a smile can reinforce a friendly
           verbal message).
        Conveyance of Interpersonal and Emotional Messages: Nonverbal
           communication conveys emotions, attitudes, and relationships (e.g., a hug can
           convey empathy and support).

Fall 2022
Assignment No. 1
Total Marks: 20
Lectures: 30-33 (Topics171-190)

Q1. Constancy under Negation Test is used to check for the presuppositions underlying sentences. It shows that the presupposition of a statement will remain constant/true even when that statement is negated.
Now, identify the correct presupposition for the given sentences.  (2*5= 10 Marks)

    1. ‘Your brother is waiting for you.’
‘Your brother is not waiting for you.’

What will be the presupposition for the above given sentences?

    a. You have to go somewhere.
    b. You have some urgent tasks to complete.
    c. You have a brother.
    d. Your brother is elder than you.

    2. ‘He ate the cheese.’
‘He didn’t eat the cheese.’

Identify the presupposition for the above given sentences?

    a. There was some cheese.
    b. He was hungry.
    c. There was nothing to eat.
    d. He had eaten too much.

    3. ‘I know why she baked a cake.’
‘I don’t know why she baked a cake.’

Identify the presupposition for the above given sentences?

    a. She is not an expert in baking.
    b. She baked a cake.
    c. She was celebrating her birthday.
    d. She ate a cake alone.

    4. ‘Carol is a better doctor than Barbara.’
‘Carol isn’t a better doctor than Barbara.’

This comparison triggers which presupposition?

    a. Carol is a quack.
    b. Carol is more competitive than Barbara.
    c. Barbara is a quack.
    d. Barbara is a doctor.

    5. ‘Debora’s cat is cute.’
‘Debora’s cat is not cute.’

Identify the presupposition for the above given sentences?

    a. Debora has a cat.
    b. Debora does not have a cat.
    c. Debora has a pair of cats.
    d. Debora’s cat is naughty.

Q2. There is either a direct or indirect relationship between the structure and the communicative function of an utterance. Identify the relationship between the form and the function of the given utterances and mark them as ‘Direct’ or ‘Indirect’ accordingly.  (2*5= 10 Marks)

    1. Please close the door.(indirect)
    2. I was wondering if Bart got the job.(indirect)
    3. Would you mind taking out the garbage?(indirect)
    4. Do you wear a seat belt?(indirect)
    5. Move out of the way!(direct)

What does Sapir's definition say about language?
Answer: Sapir defines language as a purely human, non-instinctive way of
communicating ideas, emotions, and desires using symbols.
How is "idea" in Sapir's definition problematic?
Answer: The term "idea" is vague and imprecise in Sapir's definition.
What does "non-instinctive" mean in Sapir's definition?
Answer: "Non-instinctive" means language is not inherited but learned.
Why does Sapir exclude cries and groans from his definition?
Answer: Sapir excludes cries and groans because they are involuntarily produced,
unlike voluntary symbols.
According to Sapir, what is the essence of language, and how does his
definition of language face certain limitations?
Sapir's definition of language posits that it is a uniquely human and non-
instinctive method of conveying ideas, emotions, and desires through voluntary
symbols. However, this definition is not without flaws. The terms "idea,"
"emotion," and "desire" are rather broad and may not fully encompass the range of
communication accomplished through language. The concept of "idea" especially
lacks precise definition. "Purely human" signifies that language is exclusive to
humans and distinct from animal communication. While animals do have
communication systems, they differ significantly from human language. "Non-
instinctive" denotes that language is not inherited but learned, as opposed to being
passed down genetically. Additionally, "voluntarily produced" excludes
involuntary vocalizations like cries or groans from the scope of language in this
definition.

encompasses various forms like scent, gesture, and tone.
What is the significance of each language's encoding?
Answer: Every language encodes human experience uniquely, and the loss of a
language results in the loss of a way of thinking.
How can a language be defined as a system, and what distinguishes language
from other forms of communication?
A language can be characterized as a system of arbitrary vocal symbols that
enable communication within a social group. This system comprises symbols and
rules that encompass speech sounds, writing symbols, grammar rules (e.g.,
pronouns, tense), parsing, and pragmatics. An essential aspect is the arbitrary
connection between linguistic symbols and their meanings. Language provides a
context for understanding symbols. While language is a type of communication,
it's important to differentiate between the two. Communication involves sharing
information using various mediums like scent, song, gesture, tone, writing,
painting, or language. Language specifically refers to symbolic communication.

Answer: Hall defines language as the institution through which humans

                        DISCOURSE ANALYSIS I
Topic 176: Definition

What is the example of a small favor in discourse analysis?

The phrase "Do me a favor" with a small pause.
How do big favors differ in discourse?

Big favors involve longer expressions, such as "Could you do me a favor" with
extended pauses.
What do interesting observations in discourse analysis focus on?

Observations focus on how language is used, including aspects like pauses and
language interpretation.
What questions does discourse analysis address?

COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                      1

Questions include how we make sense of what we read, recognize well-
constructed texts, understand speakers beyond literal meaning, and engage in
conversations.
Topic 177: The Origins of Discourse Analysis

Who first employed the term "discourse analysis"?

Zelling Harris first used the term to describe a method for analyzing connected
speech or writing beyond a single sentence.
How is "discourse" typically defined?

"Discourse" is defined as language beyond the sentence, focusing on the study of
language in texts and conversation.
What is the capability of language-users in understanding fragments in
newspaper headlines?

Language-users can understand the relationship between fragments, even in
headlines like "Trains collide; two die."
Topic 178: Critical Discourse Analysis

What does Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) study?

CDA studies written and spoken texts to reveal sources of power, dominance,
inequality, and bias in social, political, and historical contexts.
According to Fairclough (1993), how does CDA explore relationships?

CDA explores relationships between discursive practices, events, texts, and
broader social and cultural structures.
Topic 179: Interpreting Discourse

What is Discourse Analysis focused on in conversation?

It analyzes language 'beyond the sentence,' emphasizing the interpretation of what
speakers do in conversation.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                         2

How do language-users interpret texts that break grammatical rules?

Rather than rejecting them, users try to make sense of such texts based on their
linguistic knowledge and interpretation skills.
Topic 180: Cohesion

What is cohesion in discourse?

Cohesion is the grammatical and lexical linking within a text or sentence that gives
it meaning.
Provide examples of cohesive ties in a given text.

Examples include maintaining reference (father-he, my-I), connections between
phrases, and common elements of meaning (money, time).
Why is cohesive structure important in determining well-written texts?

Cohesive structure, including appropriate ties, is crucial in judging whether
something is well written or not.
Topic 181: Coherence

What is coherence in discourse?
Coherence is the concept of everything fitting together well beyond the text,
existing in people's understanding based on personal experiences.

Lesson-32
                      DISCOURSE ANALYSIS II

Topic 182: Discourse Typology: Spoken and Written, Formal and Informal

How does language teaching categorize discourse?

Language teaching divides discourse into two major categories: spoken and
written.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                           3

What are the subcategories under spoken and written discourse?

Subcategories include speaking and listening for spoken discourse and reading
and writing for written discourse.
How is spoken discourse different from written discourse?

Spoken discourse is less planned and more open to intervention, while written
discourse, especially formal, is often more structured.
Topic 183: Discourse and the Sentence

What is the fundamental distinction in discourse structure?

Discourse is categorized into formal and informal, where formal discourse is
planned, and informal is often spontaneous.
How is discourse different from sentences?

Discourse is language used for communication, incorporating well-formed
sentences but not limited to them.
What does discourse analysis aim to find in terms of coherence?

Discourse analysis seeks to find what gives coherence to language in
communication.
Topic 184: Discourse as Process

How is conversation described in discourse analysis?

Conversation is seen as a discourse constructed and negotiated between
participants, involving preestablished patterns, pauses, intonations, and filler
words.
What role do conventions play in discourse?

Conventions in discourse, such as turn-taking and established formulae, help
participants orientate to the interaction and make sense of it.
Topic 185: Discourse as Dialogue

According to developmental perspectives, what comes first, dialogue or
monologue?

Developmentally, dialogue comes first, preceding monologue in both the
evolution of language and individual human development.
What are some examples of early communicative skills related to dialogue?

Turn-taking and interaction, evident even in parent-infant "conversations," are
among the first communicative skills.
Topic 186: Information Structure in Discourse

What is the bi-partite structure of a clause in information structure?

A clause has a bi-partite structure, dividing information into given and new
information.
How is the ordering of information determined in discourse?

The sender's hypotheses about what the receiver knows or doesn't know dictate
the ordering of information in discourse.
Topic 187: Knowledge in Discourse: Schemata

Why is knowledge important in discourse production and comprehension?

Knowledge is crucial in discourse to predict and comprehend content; it involves

“Animals have their own intelligence and sensitivities. Many people talk to animals but a few listens to hem”. Keeping in mind the given comprehension, describe the characteristics of animal communication and why it is not considered a “language”. Your comment should not exceed 400 words.
Animal communication is rich and diverse, showcasing remarkable intelligence and sensitivity within various species. While animals communicate through intricate systems, their modes of communication possess distinct characteristics that differentiate them from human language.
Characteristics of Animal Communication:
Variety of Signals:
    • Diversity: Animals communicate through a range of signals including vocalizations, body language, scents, and visual displays.
    • Contextual Significance: These signals convey messages related to mating, warning of danger, establishing territory, or signaling distress.
Species-Specific Communication:
    • Specialization: Each species has its unique communication system tailored to its needs, often limiting the understanding of signals to members of the same species.
    • Innate or Learned: Some signals are innate, while others are learned through observation and experience.
Limited Complexity:
    • Simplicity: While some animal communication systems display complexity, they generally lack the intricate structure and grammar found in human language.
    • Fixed Repertoire: Animals often have a fixed set of signals, limiting the range and flexibility of their communication.
Contextual Nature:
Immediate and Practical: Animal communication is highly immediate and directly linked to immediate needs or environmental cues, lacking abstract or hypothetical discussions.
Why Animal Communication isn't Considered "Language":
Lack of Displacement:
    • Temporal and Spatial Limitations: Animal communication primarily focuses on the present, lacking the ability to discuss distant or abstract concepts.
    • Limited Referential Ability: Animals often cannot refer to things beyond their immediate environment or current experiences.
Grammar and Complexity:
    • Structure: While some animal communication exhibits complexity, it lacks the grammar, syntax, and generative capacity of human language.
    • Inflexibility: Animal signals often have limited combinations and lack the capacity for innovation seen in human language.
Cultural Transmission:
Limited Cultural Evolution: Animal communication tends to rely more on instinct and genetic programming rather than cultural evolution and transmission.
Conclusion:
Animal communication showcases impressive intelligence and sensitivity, but it differs significantly from human language due to its contextual nature, limited complexity, and lack of features such as displacement, complex grammar, and cultural transmission. While animals convey vital messages and exhibit sophisticated communication systems, the distinction lies in the absence of the intricate, abstract, and generative aspects that define human language.

Topic- 123: Introduction
The word ‘syntax’ comes originally from Greek and literally means ‘a putting together’ or
arrangement. There was an attempt to produce an accurate description of the sequence or ordering
‘arrangement’ of elements in the linear structure of the sentence. In the more recent attempts to
analyze syntactic structure, there has been a greater focus on the underlying rule system that we
used to produce or ‘generate’ sentences. A prepositional phrase in English consists of a preposition
followed by a noun phrase and a noun phrase consists of an article and a noun. For example, ‘near
London’ is a correct prepositional phrase as London is a proper noun and does not need an article;
on the other hand, ‘with dog’ is not a correct prepositional phrase as ‘dog’ should have article ‘a’
with it. So, the correct prepositional phrase is ‘a dog’.
Another Goal of Syntactic Analysis
A small and finite (i.e., limited) set of rules that will be capable of producing a large and potentially
infinite (i.e., unlimited) number of well-formed structures. The small and finite set of rules is
sometimes described as a ‘generative grammar’ because it can be used to ‘generate’ or produce
sentence structures and not just describe them.
Topic- 124: Generative Grammar
Generative grammar is a linguistic theory that regards grammar as a system of rules that generates
exactly those combinations of words that form grammatical sentences in a given language. The
generative school has focused on the study of syntax, but has also addressed other aspects of a
language's structure, including morphology and phonology. Early versions of Chomsky's theory
were called transformational grammar, which is still used as a general term that includes his
subsequent theories. Generativists have argued that many of the properties of a generative
grammar arise from a universal grammar that is innate to the human brain, rather than being
learned from the environment. Noam Chomsky opposed the earlier theories of structuralism by
rejecting the idea that each language is different from the other. The basic concept sets forth the
rules to recognize grammatical sentences in a language. These rules differentiate the correct
structures from improper sequences of words or ungrammatical sentences in the same language.
The sentence is represented as a tree having branches denoting the subordinate and superordinate
elements rather than just a sequence of words. Generative grammar attempts to formalize the
implicit rules that a person uses while speaking his native language. The rules of generative
grammar may appear to be useful only in language studies.
Topic- 125: Properties of Generative Grammar
Noam Chomsky has argued that many of the properties of a generative grammar arise from an
‘innate’ universal grammar, which is common to all languages. The grammar must generate all the
wellformed syntactic structures (i.e., sentences) of the language and fails to generate any ill-formed
structures. The grammar will have a finite (i.e., limited) number of rules but will be capable of
